findings.title: Bytes/Buffer field length error omits the field name
findings.description: _BytesField.__set__ raises a length error that names neither the field nor the owning Struct, unlike the sibling descriptors _StructField (names the type + value) and _UIntField/_SIntField narrowing warnings (name the field). In a record with several Buffer fields, 'expected exactly 4 bytes, got 2' gives the user no clue which field was wrong. Verified live: `s.b = b'ab'` -> `ValueError: expected exactly 4 bytes, got 2`.
findings.suggestion: Thread the field name into _BytesField (as _UIntField/_SIntField already do via self._slot.__name__[4:]) and include it: e.g. f"field {self._slot.__name__[4:]!r}: expected exactly {self._nbytes} bytes, got {len(v)}".
findings.verifyReason: Accurate and verified live. bytemaker/structs.py:254-256 raises `ValueError("expected exactly {self._nbytes} bytes, got {len(v)}")` naming neither the field nor the owning Struct. Reproduced: `s.b = b'ab'` -> `ValueError: expected exactly 4 bytes, got 2`. The sibling descriptors in the same file DO carry context: `_UIntField.__set__` (line 174) and `_SIntField.__set__` (line 197) both use `f"field {self._slot.__name__[4:]!r}"`, and `_StructField.__set__` (line 275) names the type (`expected a {self._child.__name__} instance`). So `_BytesField` is the genuine odd one out. The suggested fix is sound: I confirmed live that `S.__dict__['_bm_b'].__name__` is `'_bm_b'` and `[4:]` yields `'b'`, so the exact idiom the siblings already use works here. This is a real cross-descriptor consistency gap in a headline API, not a flag of the intentional narrative docstring style, and the fix is trivial. Downgrading severity from medium to low: the message is still correct and communicates the actual width mismatch; it is a minor polish/consistency gap (one missing detail) rather than a misleading or breaking error. Confidence stays high — all facts verified against current code and by live reproduction.

findings.title: Wrong-type store to an int field surfaces a raw operator.index TypeError with no field/struct context
findings.description: _UIntField/_SIntField.__set__ call operator.index(value) directly, so passing a str/float to an integer field (including through the generated __init__) raises Python's bare `'str' object cannot be interpreted as an integer` with no mention of the field name or the Struct. Verified live: `S('x')` and `S(3.5)` both yield `TypeError: 'str' object cannot be interpreted as an integer`, and the traceback points at codegen'd __init__, not the offending field. The string/struct/bytes descriptors all give contextual messages; the int path is the odd one out.
findings.suggestion: Wrap operator.index in try/except and re-raise with context, e.g. `raise TypeError(f"field {self._slot.__name__[4:]!r} expects an int, got {value!r}") from None`; do the same in _coerce_one for array elements.
findings.verifyReason:
Core observation verified live. `_UIntField.__set__`/`_SIntField.__set__` (bytemaker/structs.py:171, 192) call `operator.index(value)` directly, and `Array._coerce_one` (structs.py:1417) mirrors it. Passing a str/float to an int field — including via the codegen'd `__init__`, whose body is just `self.{n} = {n}` (structs.py:537) with no wrapping — raises a bare `TypeError: 'str' object cannot be interpreted as an integer` (and same for float 3.5) that points at the field descriptor, naming neither the field slot nor the Struct. Confirmed by running `S('hello')` and `S(3.5)`.

However the finding's framing is partly INACCURATE and warrants a downgrade. It claims "the string/struct/bytes descriptors all give contextual messages; the int path is the odd one out." Verified live, the FLOAT path is not contextual either: `_FloatField.__set__` (structs.py:217) does `self._ftype(float(value)).value`, so a bad value yields Python's own bare `ValueError: could not convert string to float: 'nope'` with no field/struct context — the same weakness the finding pins solely on the int path. So int is not "the odd one out"; it shares the flaw with float. Moreover the descriptors it praises are only mid-contextual: `_StructField` says `expected a Inner instance, got 123` and `_BytesField` says `expected exactly N bytes, got M` — they name the expected type but likewise never name the owning field or Struct, so "contextual" is overstated.

Severity is low, not medium: this is a wrong-type programming error at construction (not silent data corruption), Python's message does name the offending type, the file is new July code with no REF voice to violate, and the suggested fix is a polish nicety. Actionable and accurate at its core, but the comparative claim is wrong and the impact is minor.

findings.title: Array-length error message never names the offending field
findings.description: Array._coerce_seq raises a generic 'array field expects exactly N elements, got M' with no field name, so on a Struct with multiple array fields the user cannot tell which one was mis-sized. The descriptor (_ArrayField) has the field name available via its slot but does not pass it down. Verified live: `s.xs = [1,2]` on `array(UInt8, 3)` -> `ValueError: array field expects exactly 3 elements, got 2`.
findings.evidence:
raise ValueError(
    f"array field expects exactly {self._count} elements,"
    f" got {len(seq)}"
)
findings.suggestion: Pass the field name from _ArrayField.__set__ into _coerce_seq (or catch and re-raise there) so the message reads e.g. `field 'xs': array expects exactly 3 elements, got 2`.
findings.verifyReason: Accurate and fair. Verified live: on a Struct with two array fields (e.g. `xs: UInt8 * 3`, `ys: UInt8 * 2`), a wrong-length assignment `s.xs = [1, 2]` raises exactly `array field expects exactly 3 elements, got 2` (bytemaker/structs.py:1396-1399, inside Array._coerce_seq) with no field name. On a struct with two same-count array fields the messages would be indistinguishable; even with differing counts the user must reverse-engineer which field. The report's claimed mechanism is correct and there is a clear in-file precedent: the sibling scalar descriptors _UIntField/_SIntField already name the field in their diagnostics via `f"field {self._slot.__name__[4:]!r}"` (structs.py:174, 197). _ArrayField.__set__ (structs.py:376-379) holds the same `self._slot` (a __slots__ member_descriptor whose `__name__` is `_bm_<field>`) but drops it when delegating to _coerce_seq, so the fix is exactly the `[4:]`-strip pattern already used elsewhere in the module. This makes it an actionable, non-subjective in-module inconsistency, not a nitpick and not a flag of the intentional narrative docstring style. Severity is correctly low: the error is factually correct, just under-specified (diagnostic polish, not misleading behavior). Confidence high: reproduced and the enabling precedent is present in the same file.

findings.title: Float field overflow raises a codec-internal OverflowError with no field context
findings.description: _FloatField.__set__ narrows via self._ftype(float(value)).value; storing a value too large for the field width raises `OverflowError: float too large to pack with f format` from deep inside bittypes/bittype.py, naming neither the field nor the Struct. Verified live: `S(1e300)` on a Float32 field yields that traceback pointing at bittype.py line 593, not the field. (Related to the already-reported float to_binstring crashes, but the distinct DX angle here is the missing field/struct context on the _FloatField store path.)
findings.evidence: self._slot.__set__(obj, self._ftype(float(value)).value)
findings.suggestion: Catch OverflowError/ValueError from the codec cast and re-raise with the field name and the offending value, e.g. `raise ValueError(f"field {self._slot.__name__[4:]!r}: {value!r} does not fit a {self._ftype.__name__}") from exc`.
findings.verifyReason: Verified live and accurate on every checkable claim. bytemaker/structs.py:217 is exactly `self._slot.__set__(obj, self._ftype(float(value)).value)`. Reproducing `S(1e300)` on a Float32 field raises `OverflowError: float too large to pack with f format` originating at bittype.py:593 (the finding cited line 593 — exact match), naming neither the field nor the Struct. This is a genuine UX asymmetry: `_IntField.__set__` (lines 191-198) narrows out-of-range ints C-style with no error, while `_FloatField.__set__` leaks a raw codec OverflowError with no context on a plain-looking `.x = 1e300` store. This is new July code (the headline Struct API), not the intentional narrative-docstring house style, so it is not a style false-positive; and it is a distinct code path from the already-reported float to_binstring NaN/subnormal crashes. The suggested fix's `self._slot.__name__[4:]` slice is consistent with the existing pattern at line 197 and correctly recovers the field name from the `_bm_x` slot name (verified: slot.__name__ == '_bm_x'). Severity low is fair — the error type is correct and the message is technically accurate; it only bites on genuinely out-of-range float stores. Confidence high is fair given full live verification.

findings.title: array() has an endian parameter that its docstring never documents
findings.description: array() accepts keyword-only `endian` and `default`, but its one-line docstring documents neither -- it only describes the element/count and the list-checker sugar. A user reading help(array) has no way to learn that per-array byte order can be forced here (which matters: an unset array field inherits the record endianness, per the Array.__init__ note, so the override is non-obvious and undocumented). field()'s docstring likewise never mentions its `default` keyword.
findings.evidence:
def array(
    element: Any,
    count: int,
    *,
    endian: Any = None,
    default: Any = _MISSING,
) -> Any:
    """Declare a fixed-count array field: ``colors: list[int] = array(UInt16, 8)``.
    Sugar for ``field(element * count)`` with a plain-list checker type."""
findings.suggestion: Add a short param list to array()'s docstring covering `endian` (default: inherit the record's byte order) and `default`, and mention `default` in field()'s docstring.
findings.verifyReason: Accurate and fair. Verified in current code: bytemaker/structs.py array() (lines 648-657) declares keyword-only `endian` and `default`, but its two-line docstring ("Declare a fixed-count array field... Sugar for field(element * count)...") documents neither; field() (lines 631-645) likewise declares `default` but never mentions it. The `endian` omission is the load-bearing part and is not a nitpick: Array.__init__ (lines 1299-1302) explicitly documents that an unset array field inherits the record's byte order, while an explicit endian overrides it. So array(UInt16, 8, endian="little") is the sole call-site override for per-array byte order, a meaningful and non-obvious capability that help(array) gives no hint of. This is a substantive public-API documentation gap, not a complaint about the intentional narrative docstring style. Severity low is right (misleads only by omission; no false Returns/Raises and no user-facing breakage), confidence high (params are plainly undocumented). The one caveat: `default` alone is a conventional, self-explanatory keyword whose omission would be borderline trivial; the finding earns its keep chiefly on the `endian` override, which it correctly grounds.

findings.title: struct-tier pack failure surfaces a field-less 'not an integer' error
findings.description: On the aligned tier, pack_tuple first tries struct_obj.pack(*values); on TypeError/struct.error it retries with C-narrowed values. But _wrap_values only touches int-typed entries, so a bad value (None, a str, a float in an int slot) survives the retry and the SECOND struct.pack raises a raw struct.error with no field name and no offending value. A user packing a record with one mistyped field gets 'required argument is not an integer' and no clue which of their fields is at fault. Plan already knows the field names (self.fields), so this context is available but discarded.
findings.evidence: `try: return self.struct_obj.pack(*values) except (_struct.error, TypeError): return self.struct_obj.pack(*self._wrap_values(values))` (lines 245-248). Confirmed: plan.pack_tuple([5, None]) and plan.pack_tuple(['x', 3]) both raise struct.error 'required argument is not an integer' with no field identification.
findings.suggestion: On the retry's failure, catch and re-raise with per-field context, e.g. locate the first value whose type/range is wrong via self.fields/_wrap_specs and raise ValueError naming `f.name`, the value, and the expected kind/range (mirroring validate_tuple's message shape).
findings.verifyReason: Accurate and reproducible. plans.py:244-248 retries struct pack with _wrap_values (lines 261-270), which only narrows isinstance(v,int) entries, so None/str/float survive and the second struct.pack raises a raw struct.error 'required argument is not an integer' with no field name. Confirmed empirically for pack_tuple([5, None]), pack_tuple(['x', 3]), and pack_tuple([3.5, 2]). Plan does hold self.fields and validate_tuple already emits field-named messages, so the fix is cheap. However the finding's framing ("a user packing a record with one mistyped field gets no clue which field") overstates reach: the normal Struct API cannot get a bad value here. Every store goes through the field descriptor __set__ which calls operator.index(value) (structs.py:171) and rejects None/str/float at assignment time with a clear TypeError, and construction hits the same path. So the field-less struct.error is only reachable by calling plan.pack_tuple([...]) directly -- the documented bulk escape hatch (structs.py:38-41) for hot loops, which is exactly what the finding's repro does. It is a genuine, actionable rough edge on a public escape-hatch method, but because it sits behind the type-guarded everyday API its blast radius is small; low severity rather than medium.

findings.title: Plan._find KeyError gives no available-field list or record name
findings.description: bit_offset/byte_offset are the documented way to ask a Plan where a field lives. On a typo they surface KeyError('no field named 'bb''), which (a) lists neither the valid field names nor which record the plan belongs to, and (b) as a KeyError renders with confusing double-quoting in tracebacks. For an introspection helper the caller almost always wants 'did you mean...' or at least the set of names to choose from.
findings.evidence: `raise KeyError(f"no field named {name!r}")` (line 318). Confirmed: p.byte_offset('bb') raises KeyError with message "no field named 'bb'" and no list of the real names (['a','b']).
findings.suggestion: Raise a ValueError (better traceback rendering than KeyError for a message) that includes the available names, e.g. `raise ValueError(f"no field named {name!r}; fields are {[f.name for f in self.fields]}")`.
findings.verifyReason: Accurate and reproducible. bytemaker/plans.py:318 has `raise KeyError(f"no field named {name!r}")`, reached via the public introspection helpers `bit_offset` (line 320) and `byte_offset` (line 324). I reproduced it: `p.byte_offset('bb')` yields `KeyError -> "no field named 'bb'"` with no list of valid names and no record identity, and as a KeyError its str() carries the message inside its own quotes (the well-known confusing double-quote rendering in tracebacks). The finding is not a nitpick because it points at a real internal inconsistency: the sibling method `byte_offset` at line 328 already follows the better pattern — a ValueError that names the field AND adds diagnostic context (`bit {f.bit_offset}`) — so _find is the odd one out, and the suggested fix (ValueError including `[f.name for f in self.fields]`) mirrors existing in-file style. It is genuinely low severity: a mistyped-field-name lookup in an introspection helper, non-corrupting, diagnostics-quality only, not misleading docs or user-facing breakage. Confidence high on the factual claims. Not a false-positive on the intentional house narrative style (this is error-message UX, not docstring prose).

findings.title: Float aliases have no lazy factory, so `import f8`/`f128` gives a context-free AttributeError despite the docstring discussing float widths
findings.description: The module docstring explicitly discusses float widths and explains why only f16/f32/f64 exist ('an arbitrary float width does not determine an exponent/mantissa split'). But the regex only matches (u|s), so any `fN` name — a natural thing for a user to try given uN/sN 'just work' — falls straight through to the generic `raise AttributeError(f"module {__name__!r} has no attribute {name!r}")`. The user gets no hint that floats are a fixed IEEE set or that f16/f32/f64 are the supported spellings. The knowledge to give a helpful message lives right there in the docstring but is not surfaced in the error.
findings.evidence: raise AttributeError(f"module {__name__!r} has no attribute {name!r}")   # regex: r"(u|s)([1-9][0-9]*)" never matches an f-prefixed name
findings.suggestion: Detect an f-prefixed numeric name in __getattr__ (e.g. a second regex r"f([0-9]+)") and raise an AttributeError that says float aliases are the fixed IEEE set {f16, f32, f64} because an arbitrary float width has no defined exponent/mantissa split, pointing the user at those names or at Float.specialize for custom splits.
findings.verifyReason: Accurate and reachable. In bytemaker/fields.py the lazy factory `__getattr__` (lines 88-91) matches only `_ALIAS_PATTERN = re.compile(r"(u|s)([1-9][0-9]*)")` (line 83), so f-prefixed numeric names fall through to the generic `raise AttributeError(f"module {__name__!r} has no attribute {name!r}")` (line 91). I confirmed empirically: `getattr(fields, "f8")`, `"f128"`, `"f31")` all raise "module 'bytemaker.fields' has no attribute 'f8'" with no hint, while `u31`/`s5` resolve via specialize. The asymmetry is genuine: the module docstring (lines 8-17) advertises that arbitrary `uN`/`sN` "just work" and explicitly explains floats are the fixed IEEE set f16/f32/f64 because "an arbitrary float width does not determine an exponent/mantissa split" — yet that knowledge is not surfaced in the error a user hits when they reach for `f8`. This is a real UX gap, not a style nitpick or the intentional narrative-docstring style. One imprecision in the report: via `from bytemaker.fields import f8` Python's import machinery wraps the AttributeError into an ImportError ("cannot import name 'f8'"), so the quoted message text is exactly what's seen only on direct attribute/getattr access, not the `from ... import` form the title uses — but the substance (context-free, unhelpful error) holds either way. Downgrading severity from medium to low: the user does get a correct error (the attribute genuinely doesn't exist); this is a missing helpful-hint / nice-to-have improvement, not a doc that actively misleads or a breakage. The suggestion (a second f-prefix regex with a targeted message) is concrete and actionable. Confidence high that the behavior is exactly as described.

findings.title: N * Cls array sugar fails with a cryptic Int.__mul__ arity error
findings.description: BitTypeMeta advertises array sugar ("cls * N -> Array", "UInt16 * 257"). The reflected form N * Cls (e.g. 257 * UInt16) is a natural thing to try, but __rmul__ delegates via cls.__mul__(count). On a class object, cls.__mul__ resolves to the INSTANCE numeric operator (Int.__mul__ from the value ops), not the metaclass array-sugar __mul__. So 4 * UInt8 raises "TypeError: Int.__mul__() missing 1 required positional argument: 'other'" instead of building an Array — a confusing, internals-leaking error for a documented-feeling operation.
findings.evidence: Code: "def __rmul__(cls, count: int):\n        return cls.__mul__(count)". Runtime: `4 * UInt8` → "TypeError: Int.__mul__() missing 1 required positional argument: 'other'". `UInt8.__mul__` resolves to `<function Int.__mul__>`, not `BitTypeMeta.__mul__`.
findings.suggestion: Dispatch through the metaclass explicitly: `return type(cls).__mul__(cls, count)` (or inline `from bytemaker.structs import Array; return Array.of(cls, count)`). Add a test for `N * Cls`.
findings.verifyReason:
Accurate and runtime-verified. bytemaker/bittypes/bittype.py:79-80: `def __rmul__(cls, count): return cls.__mul__(count)`. Testing `4 * UInt8` raises `TypeError: Int.__mul__() missing 1 required positional argument: 'other'`, exactly as claimed. Root cause confirmed: `UInt8.__mul__` resolves to `<function Int.__mul__>` (the instance value operator in the class's own MRO), not `BitTypeMeta.__mul__` (the metaclass array sugar), because class-object attribute lookup searches the class MRO before the metaclass. I also traced that `BitTypeMeta.__rmul__` IS actually reached at runtime, so this is a live, intended feature (reflected `N * Cls`) that is silently broken by an implementation bug — not dead code. The suggested fix `type(cls).__mul__(cls, count)` is verified to correctly produce an Array. Not a nitpick and not the intentional house docstring style; it is a genuine ergonomics defect with an internals-leaking error message.

Severity downgraded from medium to low: the docstring (bittype.py:69-72) only advertises the forward form (`cls * N`, e.g. `UInt16 * 257`), which works correctly. `N * Cls` is a natural thing to try and its failure is confusing, but it is a secondary reflected-operator path, not breakage of any documented example or the happy path. Confidence remains high — the behavior is deterministic and directly reproduced.

findings.title: NarrowingConfig/NarrowingWarning defined here but not exported from bittypes package
findings.description: NarrowingConfig and NarrowingWarning are defined in bittypes/bittype.py and their own docstrings instruct users to enable checked stores "via NarrowingConfig" and to escalate with warnings.simplefilter('error', NarrowingWarning). Yet neither symbol is re-exported by bittypes/__init__.py (not imported, not in __all__). `from bytemaker.bittypes import NarrowingConfig` raises ImportError, even though they live in that subpackage. They are only reachable from the top-level `bytemaker` package and from structs.py, which is a discoverability inconsistency: the knob is documented next to its definition but not importable from the package that defines it.
findings.evidence: `from bytemaker.bittypes import NarrowingConfig` → "ImportError: cannot import name 'NarrowingConfig' from 'bytemaker.bittypes'". bittype.py docstring: "Enable via :class:`NarrowingConfig` ... warnings.simplefilter(\"error\", NarrowingWarning)". __init__.py imports from .bittype only "BitType, StructPackedBitType, bytes_to_bittype" and __all__ omits the narrowing symbols.
findings.suggestion: Add NarrowingConfig and NarrowingWarning to the `from bytemaker.bittypes.bittype import ...` line and to __all__ in bittypes/__init__.py, matching the top-level bytemaker package which already exports them.
findings.verifyReason: Verified against current code. In bytemaker/bittypes/bittype.py, NarrowingWarning (line 27) and NarrowingConfig (line 39) are defined, and their docstrings direct users to them by name: line 32 "Enable via :class:`NarrowingConfig`" and lines 33-35 "warnings.simplefilter(\"error\", NarrowingWarning)". Yet bytemaker/bittypes/__init__.py line 1 imports only "BitType, StructPackedBitType, bytes_to_bittype" from .bittype, and __all__ (lines 65-125) omits both narrowing symbols, so `from bytemaker.bittypes import NarrowingConfig` raises ImportError. The asymmetry is confirmed: the top-level bytemaker/__init__.py DOES import (lines 58-59) and export (lines 72-73) both. This is a genuine, evidence-backed discoverability inconsistency, not a flag of the intentional narrative docstring style. It is accurate and the suggested one-line fix is reasonable. It is fairly minor, though: the knob remains reachable from the canonical top-level `bytemaker` package and from its defining module, and a subpackage __init__ exposing a curated subset is a common, defensible pattern; the docstrings name the symbol but do not promise a specific import path, so they do not strictly lie. Low severity is the fair calibration; confidence is high because the ImportError and the export asymmetry are directly verifiable in the source.

findings.title: to_bits/from_bits are marked DEPRECATED in docstrings but emit no DeprecationWarning
findings.description: Both to_bits() and from_bits() open their docstrings with "DEPRECATED" and point to the replacement (the `bits` property / the constructor), but neither issues a runtime DeprecationWarning. A developer who never opens the source (the common case for deprecated helpers) gets no signal to migrate; the deprecation is invisible outside the docstring. This weakens the migration path the maintainer clearly intends (the methods are even tagged "# TODO remove").
findings.evidence: Docstrings begin "DEPRECATED\n        Use the `bits` property instead." and "DEPRECATED\n        Use the constructor ... instead." Running both under -W all with a warnings recorder emits 0 warnings.
findings.suggestion: Emit `warnings.warn("BitType.to_bits() is deprecated; use the .bits property", DeprecationWarning, stacklevel=2)` (and the analog for from_bits) so the deprecation is discoverable at runtime, or remove the methods per the TODO.
findings.verifyReason: Accurate and fair. Verified in bytemaker/bittypes/bittype.py:350-372: to_bits() and from_bits() docstrings both open with "DEPRECATED" pointing to replacements ("Use the `bits` property instead." / "Use the constructor with a BitVector-like object instead."), sit under a "# TODO remove" comment (line 349), yet their bodies merely delegate (return self.bits / return cls(bits=bits)) with no runtime signal. Empirically confirmed: calling both under `python -W all` with simplefilter('always') emits 0 warnings. This is a real UX gap, not a nitpick and not the intentional narrative-docstring style: a developer who never opens the source gets no migration signal. It is strengthened by the fact that the same module already imports and uses warnings.warn (line 52, for NarrowingWarning), so the idiomatic mechanism is present but unapplied here. One caveat, which keeps severity low and nuances the suggestion: these "deprecated" methods are still called by bytemaker's own hot legacy path (_legacy_aggregate.py:121 `unit.to_bits()` and :176 `unittype.from_bits(...)`), so naively adding a DeprecationWarning would fire on every legacy aggregate (de)serialization internally — the finding's alternative suggestion (remove per the TODO after redirecting those internal callers) is the cleaner fix. Low/high severity/confidence are appropriate: the docstring is truthful (not actively misleading) and this is a small deprecated helper, so it is polish rather than breakage, but the claim itself is solid.

findings.title: min_bit_length silently returns None for an unrecognized signed bin_format, causing a cryptic downstream TypeError
findings.description: In the signed branch of min_bit_length there is no final else that raises for an unknown bin_format: the if/elif chain covers only twos_complement, signed/sign_magnitude, and ones_complement, then the function falls off the end and returns None. Every sibling code path (the unsigned branch, to_bitstring, to_pyint) raises ValueError('Unsupported format: ...') on a bad format, so this one is inconsistent and, worse, the None it returns flows into to_bitstring as bit_length and blows up far from the mistake. Calling Int.to_bitstring(5, signed=True, rep_format='garbage') (bit_length left to default) raises 'TypeError: <= not supported between instances of NoneType and int' at the 'if bit_length <= 0' check instead of a clear format error. (Pre-existing: the ref_4wks min_bit_length also lacked the raise, so this is not new July regression, but it is a genuine DX footgun in this file.)
findings.evidence:
elif bin_format == "ones_complement":
    if n == 0:
        return 1  # ...
    return ceil(log2(abs(n) + 1)) + 1
# (no trailing `else: raise` — an unknown signed bin_format returns None)

# downstream effect, observed:
#   Int.to_bitstring(5, signed=True, rep_format='garbage')
#   -> TypeError: '<=' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'int'
findings.suggestion: Add a final `else: raise ValueError(f"Unsupported format: {bin_format!r}. Expected one of 'twos_complement', 'signed_magnitude', 'ones_complement'.")` to the signed branch of min_bit_length so an unknown format fails immediately at the source with a clear, choice-listing message instead of returning None and surfacing as a NoneType TypeError later.
findings.verifyReason: Accurate and reproduced. In bytemaker/bittypes/int.py the signed branch of min_bit_length (lines 169-195) is an if/elif chain covering twos_complement, signed_magnitude/sign_magnitude, and ones_complement with no final `else: raise`, so an unrecognized bin_format falls off the end and returns None. I ran it live: Int.min_bit_length(5, signed=True, bin_format='garbage') returns None, and Int.to_bitstring(5, signed=True, rep_format='garbage') raises "TypeError: '<=' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'int'" at the `if bit_length <= 0` check (line 288) after min_bit_length feeds None into bit_length (line 286) — exactly as claimed. The inconsistency claim also holds: the sibling paths from_bitstring/to_pyint (lines 137-138) and to_bitstring (lines 301-302) both end their format dispatch with `else: raise ValueError(f"Unsupported format: ...")`, while min_bit_length does not. This is a real DX footgun (a function annotated `-> int` can return None; failure surfaces far from the cause with a cryptic message) and the suggested one-line fix is correct and actionable. It is a behavior finding, not a flag of the intentional narrative docstring style. findings.title: Bogus encoding= name accepted at mint, fails late at first encode/decode
findings.description: When encoding= is a str, of() stashes it as encoding_name with no validation. An unknown codec name (typo like 'utf-99') mints a working-looking type; the failure only appears at the first encode/decode as a bare `LookupError: unknown encoding: utf-99` with no reference to the field or String class. The rest of of() is careful to fail early with class-named messages, so this is an inconsistency and a discoverability trap for the common typo case.

Reproduced: `String.of(nbytes=4, encoding='utf-99')` mints; `T('AB')` raises `LookupError: unknown encoding: utf-99`.

Verified against current code: bytemaker/bittypes/string.py:445-447 stashes a str encoding= as `encoding_name` with no validation (`elif isinstance(encoding, str): base = StandardEncodingString; ns["encoding_name"] = encoding`), and line 473-474 (`return BitVector(value.encode(cls.encoding_name))`) is where the bogus name first bites. The suggested fix (codecs.lookup(encoding) at mint) is correct and actionable. Not a style nit and not flagging the intentional narrative docstrings. Severity low and confidence high both stand.

findings.title: String/Buffer repr shows raw bits and an endianness that is meaningless for text/byte fields, not the round-trippable value
findings.description: String and Buffer inherit BitType.__str__/__repr__, which render `bits=FixedLengthBitVector('01101000 ...')` and an `[big]` endianness tag. For a text field the string value is what a developer needs to see; the bit soup is unreadable and the endianness label is misleading (a String's wire contract is bytes, not an endian-swappable integer). repr() is supposed to help debugging, and for these types it actively hides the useful value.
findings.evidence: Inherited from BitType (bittype.py lines 237-264). Observed: `str(UTF8String.of(nbytes=8)('hello'))` -> `UTF8Stringx8[big](hello = 01101000...00000000)` and `repr(...)` -> `UTF8Stringx8(bits=FixedLengthBitVector('01101000 01100101 ...'), endianness=big)` -- the human-readable 'hello' appears only in str, never in repr, and the [big] tag has no meaning for text.
findings.suggestion: Override __repr__ on String (and consider Buffer) to lead with the decoded value, e.g. `UTF8Stringx8('hello')` or include the value alongside a hex byte dump, and drop the endianness tag for types whose wire form is a byte sequence rather than an endian-swapped scalar.
findings.verifyReason:
Verified empirically. Running `repr(UTF8String.of(nbytes=8)('hello'))` yields `UTF8Stringx8(bits=FixedLengthBitVector('01101000 01100101 01101100 01101100 01101111 00000000 00000000 00000000'), endianness=big)` and `str(...)` yields `UTF8Stringx8[big](hello = 01101000...00000000)`. Both match the finding's claimed output exactly. String and Buffer inherit BitType.__str__/__repr__ (bittype.py:237-264) with no override; the decoded 'hello' appears only in str, never in repr, and repr is conventionally meant to surface the reconstructable/useful value. This is a genuine debugging-UX gap: for a text field the developer must mentally decode bit-soup to see the value.

The finding is accurate, actionable (concrete suggestion to override __repr__ on String/Buffer), and NOT merely flagging the intentional house narrative docstring style (it concerns runtime repr/str output). It is distinct from all ALREADY-REPORTED items. Not a nitpick: repr hiding the meaningful value is a real convention violation.

Two calibration notes keeping this at low/high rather than higher: (1) it is a cosmetic repr/str issue on secondary types with no data-corruption or breakage impact, so low severity is correct. (2) The endianness-tag half of the argument ("meaningless for text") is a softer design opinion — endianness is a legitimate attribute every BitType carries and String does accept it; the string.py comments (lines 63-64, 379-380) do confirm the wire contract stays bytes with no endian swap, which supports the reviewer, but 'misleading' is a judgment call rather than a clear bug. The core claim (repr hides the decoded value for text/byte types) is unambiguously real, hence high confidence.

findings.title: Equal-length bitwise error omits the two actual lengths

findings.title: Invalid construction source raises ValueError (not TypeError) and omits the offending value

A wrong *type* is conventionally a TypeError, so `except TypeError` around a constructor will miss it. The message prints the class but not the value; for a mistyped literal the value is the more useful diagnostic.

findings.suggestion: Raise TypeError and include a hint at accepted forms, e.g. raise TypeError(f"cannot construct BitVector from {source!r} of type {type(source).__name__}; expected BitVector, bytes, str, an int size, an iterable of 0/1, or a BitsCastable").

findings.title: pop() 'from empty' message is misleading for non-empty out-of-range indexes
findings.description: The guard fires for ANY out-of-bounds index (`index >= len(self) or index < 0`), but the raised message always says 'pop from empty BitVector'. Calling `BitVector('1111').pop(99)` on a non-empty 4-bit vector reports it as empty, which actively misleads the user about what went wrong (index too large vs. no bits). The offending index and the actual length are both known but omitted. The bitarray backend shares the same defect (bitvector_with_bitarray_speedup.py:1086-1089).
findings.suggestion: Raise a message that reflects the real condition and includes context, e.g. `raise IndexError(f"pop index {index} out of range for BitVector of length {len(self)}")`, and only say 'empty' when len(self) == 0.
findings.verifyReason:
Accurate and real. Verified in current code: bytemaker/bitvector/bitvector_native.py:1157-1160 guards `if index >= len(self) or index < 0:` and unconditionally raises `IndexError("pop from empty BitVector")`, and bytemaker/bitvector/bitvector_with_bitarray_speedup.py:1086-1089 does the same with `IndexError("pop from empty bitarray")`. So BitVector('1111').pop(99) on a non-empty vector reports "pop from empty", misdiagnosing an out-of-range index as an empty container. The method's own docstring (lines 1137-1141, 1070-1082) frames the condition as general "out of bounds", and Python's list distinguishes "pop from empty list" from "pop index out of range", so this is a genuine, user-facing message defect, not the intentional house narrative style and not a docstring nit. The suggested fix (include index and length, reserve "empty" for len==0) is concrete and correct.

Two caveats that reduce it from medium to low. First, a report inaccuracy: it claims the bitarray backend uses "pop from empty BitVector" too, but that backend actually says "pop from empty bitarray" — the defect is real but the quoted evidence for the second file is slightly wrong. Second, this is error-message wording only: the code always still raises IndexError and never returns a wrong value or silently mis-behaves, so the practical harm is limited to a confusing message during debugging. That is real but polish-level, so severity is fairly low (confidence high that it is present and genuinely misleading). Note: this lives in the mature, reference-era BitVector code (the reference tree's compiled .pyc contains the same "pop from empty" string), so it is a long-standing issue rather than new July churn.

findings.title: pop(default=...) silently swallows out-of-range errors, a silent-wrong footgun
findings.description: pop() accepts a `default` and returns it whenever the index is out of bounds, so `bv.pop(500, default=0)` returns 0 instead of raising, even though the caller almost certainly has a bug. Worse, because default defaults to None but the guard tests `if default is not None`, the API can't distinguish 'no default given' from 'default is None'; the branch is only taken for non-None defaults. list.pop/bytearray.pop have no such signature, so this both surprises users familiar with the stdlib and can silently mask indexing bugs. The bitarray backend has the same signature (bitvector_with_bitarray_speedup.py:1063-1090).
findings.suggestion: Either drop the non-standard `default` parameter to match list/bytearray semantics, or use a sentinel (`_MISSING`) so an explicit `default=None` is honored and 'no default' still raises; document that a default suppresses IndexError.
findings.verifyReason:
Confirmed in current code. bitvector_native.py:1134-1163 has `pop(self, index=None, default: Optional[T] = None)` with guard `if default is not None: return default` else raise IndexError; the bitarray backend at bitvector_with_bitarray_speedup.py:1063-1090 is identical. The evidence quote matches exactly.

The finding bundles a strong claim and a weak one. WEAK (subjective): framing the whole `default` param as a "silent-wrong footgun" that "surprises users familiar with the stdlib." The default-suppresses-lookup-error pattern is idiomatic Python (`dict.pop(k, default)`, `getattr(obj, name, default)`), it is explicitly documented ("If a default is provided and the index is out of bounds, the default is returned"), and structs.py:1180-1186 deliberately propagates the contract with a comment. So it is an intentional API choice, not an accident, and the list.pop comparison is not the right analogue.

STRONG (real defect): the sentinel bug. Signature default is `None` but the guard tests `if default is not None`, so an explicit `default=None` cannot be honored — `bv.pop(500, default=None)` raises IndexError instead of returning None, contradicting the docstring's "the default is returned" and the Raises clause's "no default provided." The suggested `_MISSING` sentinel is the correct fix. This is a concrete, objective inconsistency present in both backends, and it is actually reachable since structs.py:1184 forwards `default` through.

Net: real and actionable on the sentinel/None inconsistency; downgraded because the headline "footgun" framing is editorialized about an intentional, idiomatic feature. Severity stays low (impact limited to the rare case of passing default=None explicitly). Confidence raised to high — the sentinel defect is unambiguously in the code.

findings.title: __contains__ falls through to an implicit None return instead of a bool
findings.description: __contains__ is declared `-> bool` but its final branch is guarded by `if isinstance(item, bitarray):` with no `else`, so any path reaching line 882 where item is not a bitarray returns None. Python coerces the None to False for the `in` operator, so it happens to behave, but the method is fragile: any future edit that lets a non-bitarray reach the tail silently yields a wrong membership answer with no error. The native sibling instead ends with an `assert isinstance(item, BitVector)` then a plain `return first_index != -1` (bitvector_native.py:908-910), which is safer.
findings.evidence: if isinstance(item, bitarray):\n            first_index = self.find(item)\n            return first_index != -1   (no final return; method falls off the end returning None)
findings.suggestion: Add an explicit `return False` after the block (or restructure to the native backend's assert-then-return form) so every path returns a genuine bool.
findings.verifyReason: Verified accurate. In bytemaker/bitvector/bitvector_with_bitarray_speedup.py, __contains__ is declared `-> bool` (line 864) and its tail is guarded by `if isinstance(item, bitarray):` (lines 882-884) with no else, so a path reaching line 882 with a non-bitarray item would fall off the end and return None. Every factual claim checks out: I traced all four control-flow paths and confirmed that in the CURRENT code no reachable path leaves item as a non-bitarray (the int branch reassigns to BitVector, which subclasses bitarray per line 97; the elif reassigns or returns False; a bare bitarray skips the elif). So the method "happens to behave" today, exactly as the finding states, and the None-fall-through is latent, not a live bug. The native sibling (bitvector_native.py lines 908-910) genuinely closes the same logic with `assert isinstance(item, BitVector)` then an unconditional `return first_index != -1`, so the inconsistency between the two behaviorally-interchangeable backends is real and concrete, not a subjective style nit and not the intentional narrative-docstring style. The fix is a trivial one-line `return False` (or matching the native assert-then-return form). Fair and actionable, correctly self-rated low severity since there is no user-facing breakage. findings.title: bytes/bytearray/memoryview conversions look registered but are dead (registration commented out)
findings.description: The loop over [bytes, bytearray, memoryview] constructs a ConversionInfo each iteration but its ConversionConfig.set_conversion_info call is commented out, so none of these types are actually registered. The code reads as live (a for-loop building conversion_info), yet converting a bytes value fails with a generic 'No conversion found' error that gives no hint these types were deliberately excluded. findings.title: pytype conversion functions misname/mistype their instance parameter as `type`
findings.description: pytype_to_bits/pytype_to_bytes take a value instance to serialize, but the parameter is named py_prim and annotated `type`, and the docstrings call it 'The python instance' while the signature says type. (1) pytype_to_bytes (line 281-282): `def pytype_to_bytes(py_prim: type, ...)` annotates the param `type`, but the docstring (line 289) says "py_prim: The python instance to convert to bytes" and the body passes py_prim (a value) into pytype_to_bits. In all three the `type` annotation / `(type)` parenthetical directly contradicts both the prose docstring and the runtime contract, which would mislead type-checkers and autocomplete into suggesting callers pass `int` rather than an int value. findings.title: Stub (.pyi) caps uN/sN at width 64 while the runtime supports any width, so checked code past 64 silently loses precise typing
findings.description: The runtime module mints uN/sN for arbitrary N (u128, u256, u1000), and canonical BitType classes exist up to 128/256. The stub only declares u1..u64 and s1..s64 as descriptor classes; everything else falls to `def __getattr__(name: str) -> Any: ...`. The stub itself admits this ('Widths past 64 resolve at runtime via the module __getattr__; they type as Any here'), but the effect is a silent DX cliff: `x: u128` type-checks as a bare descriptor/Any and the read/write channel typing (int on read, SupportsIndex on write) that u1..u64 get is lost exactly for the wide fields where a mistyped huge literal is most likely. The .py/.pyi 'must agree' expectation (unit hint) holds only up to 64.
findings.evidence: "Widths past 64 resolve at runtime via the module __getattr__; they type as\nAny here."  ...  class u64(_UIntAlias): ...   (no u65+)   ...   def __getattr__(name: str) -> Any: ...
findings.suggestion: Either document the 64-bit typing cliff more prominently at the alias-usage site, or make the stub __getattr__ return a descriptor-typed alias (e.g. -> _UIntAlias) for u/s names so wide fields still type reads as int and writes as SupportsIndex instead of degrading to Any.
findings.verifyReason:
Verified against current code. The runtime (bytemaker/fields.py:88-111, docstring line 8 "Any integer width works") genuinely mints uN/sN for arbitrary N — confirmed empirically: `bytemaker.fields.u128` -> `Annotated[int, UInt128]`, `s200` -> a minted SInt specialization. The stub bytemaker/fields.pyi only declares descriptor classes for u1..u64 and s1..s64 (lines 28-156); everything else routes through `def __getattr__(name: str) -> Any: ...` (line 162). So `x: u128` type-checks as Any, losing the read-as-int / write-as-SupportsIndex channel typing that u1..u64 get from the _UIntAlias/_SIntAlias descriptors. This is a real, actionable typing gap and the suggested fix (stub __getattr__ returning a descriptor-typed _UIntAlias/_SIntAlias for u/s names) is sound. It is not a house-style nitpick and does not flag the intentional narrative docstring style.

Downgraded confidence from high to medium because the finding slightly overstates the impact: (1) the cliff is NOT truly "silent" — the stub docstring (fields.pyi:9-11) explicitly states "Widths past 64 resolve at runtime via the module __getattr__; they type as Any here", a location the user sees on hover/import; (2) the failure mode is only loss of extra checking (fields degrade to permissive Any, never to a wrong type, and no runtime behavior changes); (3) wide (>64-bit) fields are a niche case, and the "mistyped huge literal is most likely there" rationale is speculative; (4) the finding's ".py/.pyi must agree" framing is loose — the runtime provides Annotated[int, BitType] while the stub provides descriptor classes, so the two representations already deliberately differ (documented in fields.py:19-22). Severity low is fair; the issue is minor DX polish, well-scoped, and already partly documented.

findings.title: Bitwise binary operators refuse silently with no hint, unlike __invert__
findings.description: The module deliberately disables value-plane bitwise ops and the code comment (lines 357-360) promises 'the bit-plane spelling is explicit: f.bits & other'. __invert__ delivers exactly that guidance in its TypeError. But the ten binary/shift dunders just return NotImplemented, so the user who types `f & 3` or `f << 2` gets Python's generic "unsupported operand type(s) for &: 'Float32' and 'int'" with no pointer to the f.bits spelling. The result is an inconsistent DX: unary ~ teaches the workaround, the far more commonly attempted binary & / | / ^ / << / >> do not, even though the whole point of overriding them was to steer users to the bit-plane spelling.
findings.evidence: Lines 362-390 each 'return NotImplemented' (e.g. 'def __and__(self, other):\n        return NotImplemented'). Contrast __invert__ (lines 392-396): raise TypeError(... '(the bit-plane spelling is ~self.bits)'). Observed: `f & 3` -> TypeError "unsupported operand type(s) for &: 'Float32' and 'int'" (no hint); `~f` -> TypeError "... (the bit-plane spelling is ~self.bits)".
findings.suggestion: Either raise a TypeError from these ops with the same teaching hint (e.g. 'bitwise & is not defined on Float values; use f.bits & other for the bit plane'), consistent with __invert__, or add that guidance to the class docstring so at least one discoverable place documents the f.bits workaround.
findings.verifyReason: Accurate and reproducible. In bytemaker/bittypes/float.py, the ten binary/shift dunders (lines 362-390) each `return NotImplemented`, while `__invert__` (lines 392-396) raises `TypeError(... "(the bit-plane spelling is ~self.bits)")`. I confirmed the runtime behavior on a Float32 instance: `~f` -> "bad operand type for unary ~: 'Float32' (the bit-plane spelling is ~self.bits)", but `f & 3`, `f | 3`, `f ^ 3`, `f << 2`, `f >> 2` all give Python's generic "unsupported operand type(s) for ...: 'Float32' and 'int'" with no pointer to f.bits. The class docstring (lines 22-54) does not document the f.bits spelling anywhere, so there is no discoverable place teaching the workaround for the commonly-attempted binary ops. This is new July code (no float.py existed in the REF tree), so the asymmetry reads as an oversight, not a deliberate legacy artifact. The finding is a real DX inconsistency with a clean, low-risk fix (document f.bits in the class docstring), so it is not a nitpick to reject. Two caveats keep it firmly at low severity and lower the confidence to medium: (1) the "promise" it leans on (lines 357-360) is an internal source comment, not user-facing documentation, so users never actually saw a broken promise; (2) the finding does not acknowledge that `return NotImplemented` from binary dunders is idiomatic Python that correctly preserves the reflected-operand protocol, which is a legitimate reason binary ops differ from unary __invert__ -- so its primary suggested fix (raising a custom TypeError from __and__ et al.) is debatable, and only its secondary suggestion (docstring guidance) is clearly good. Worth a low-priority polish note, framed as documentation rather than as a broken promise.

findings.title: specialize() leaks trailing-underscore parameter names into the public signature
findings.description: specialize is a public, documented factory (referenced by the class docstring as the way to make custom widths), but every parameter carries an internal trailing underscore (num_exponent_bits_, num_mantissa_bits_, packing_format_letter_, name_) because the body reuses the bare names for the class-body assignments. A user calling it by keyword must write the ugly Float.specialize(num_exponent_bits_=5, num_mantissa_bits_=10), and inspect.signature / IDE autocomplete surface the underscored names. The prose in the docstring even refers to them without the underscore ('If `packing_format_letter` is provided', line 225), so the documented name and the real keyword disagree.
findings.evidence: Signature (lines 214-220): 'def specialize(cls, num_exponent_bits_, num_mantissa_bits_, packing_format_letter_: Optional[str] = None, name_: Optional[str] = None,)'. inspect.signature(Float.specialize) -> '(num_exponent_bits_, num_mantissa_bits_, packing_format_letter_: 'Optional[str]' = None, name_: 'Optional[str]' = None)'. Docstring line 225 says '`packing_format_letter`' (no underscore).
findings.suggestion: Rename the public parameters to num_exponent_bits / num_mantissa_bits / packing_format_letter / name and assign them into locals for the nested class body (e.g. `_nexp = num_exponent_bits`), so the public keyword names are clean and match the prose.
findings.verifyReason:
The finding's headline thesis is UNFAIR, but it contains one genuine, salvageable sub-defect. Verified in current code:

WHAT'S REAL (and float-specific): float.py:225 docstring says `packing_format_letter` (no underscore) while the actual parameter is `packing_format_letter_` (float.py:218). That documented keyword name disagrees with the real keyword — a genuine doc-vs-signature mismatch. The sibling specialize() docstrings do NOT have this: int.py:625 uses plain prose ("If a packing format letter is provided"), and every Args block elsewhere keeps the underscore. So float.py is the odd one out on this one line. Worth a one-character fix.

WHAT'S UNFAIR (the finding's primary framing): The finding treats the trailing-underscore parameter names as a float.py UX defect to be renamed. But this is a deliberate, uniform HOUSE CONVENTION across the entire bittypes package — string.py:339 (num_bits_, name_), buffer.py:60 (num_bits_, name_), int.py:616 SInt (num_bits_, packing_format_letter_, name_), int.py:801 UInt (same), and float.py all use it. The docstrings consistently document the underscored names (int.py:632-637, buffer.py:64-67). A user calling ANY of these by keyword must use the underscore, so nothing is float-specific about the "ugly Float.specialize(num_exponent_bits_=5)" claim. The suggested fix (rename float's params to clean names, assign to locals) would break the package-wide uniformity and INTRODUCE inconsistency rather than remove it — the opposite of the finding's stated goal.

Net: real=true because a concrete, float-specific docstring/param mismatch exists at line 225, but the finding is downgraded: its "leaks trailing-underscore names into the public signature / rename the parameters" thesis mischaracterizes an intentional convention as a bug, and its suggestion is wrong. The only actionable, fair fix is aligning line 225's backtick reference to `packing_format_letter_` (add the underscore) to match the signature and the rest of its own Args block. Severity stays low; confidence medium (the line-225 mismatch is solid; the broader claim is not).

findings.title: String base class has no docstring while every sibling BitType does; base String not exported as a mint entry point

Promote the field-knob comment (pad/terminator/strip/errors/truncate/bytes_per_char) into the docstring so help() and tooltips surface it.

However the finding is overstated on two points, warranting medium (not high) confidence: (1) the knobs are NOT "documented only in a code comment" — the String.of() classmethod at line 349 carries a thorough docstring (lines 363-393) documenting nbytes/nchars/bytes_per_char/encoding/pad/terminator/strip/errors/truncate, so the API is discoverable via help(String.of), just not via help(String); (2) the title's second clause "base String not exported as a mint entry point" is factually wrong — String IS exported: it appears in string.py's __all__ (line 561), is imported in bittypes/__init__.py (line 60) and re-exported in its __all__ (line 121). findings.title: FixedLengthBitVector length-violation message does not name the attempted operation
findings.description: A single _length_violation() helper is reused across append, extend, insert, pop, remove, clear, __delitem__, __iadd__, __imul__, frombytes, fromfile, and __setitem__. The resulting ValueError always reads "width-changing mutation is not allowed" without naming which call triggered it, so in a stack of chained operations the user cannot tell whether it was e.g. `+=` vs `.append` vs a resizing slice assignment without inspecting the traceback frame.
findings.suggestion: Pass the operation name into the helper (def _length_violation(self, op): ...) and interpolate it, e.g. "append() would change the length ... FixedLengthBitVector length is invariant (N bits)".
findings.verifyReason: Accurate as to the code: bytemaker/bitvector/fixed.py:33-38 defines a single `_length_violation()` helper reused verbatim by append/extend/insert/pop/remove/clear/__delitem__/__iadd__/__imul__/frombytes/fromfile/__setitem__ (lines 40-88), and the ValueError message never names the triggering operation. The quote matches exactly. So the finding is real, not fabricated, and the suggestion (thread an `op` name into the helper) is actionable. However it is a marginal low-value polish item and I downgrade confidence for two reasons the report underweights: (1) the existing message is already unusually informative for this codebase — it states the invariant, the current width, and the exact remedy ("make a resizable copy with BitVector(...) first"), well above the terse norm of sibling messages like "pop from empty BitVector" or "negative shift count" which also don't name operations; (2) the report's core premise — that "the user cannot tell whether it was `+=` vs `.append`" without extra effort — is weak, because each of these is a distinct method/statement whose name and source line appear in the top frame of the standard traceback that always accompanies the raised ValueError, so the operation identity is already surfaced for free. It's a fair, honest low/low suggestion but sits at the nitpick boundary rather than being clearly worth the maintainer's attention.

findings.title: classproperty getter/setter/deleter AttributeErrors omit the attribute name
findings.description: classproperty raises 'unreadable attribute', "can't set attribute", and "can't delete attribute" with no attribute name. Python's own built-in property was upgraded in 3.11 to include the attribute name (e.g. "property 'x' of 'C' object has no setter"). On a class with several classproperties, a bare "can't set attribute" forces the developer to hunt for which one they touched. Since __get__ already receives objtype, the class and attribute are available to name.
findings.suggestion: Include context, e.g. raise AttributeError(f"unreadable classproperty on {objtype.__name__}") and f"can't set classproperty on {type(obj).__name__}", matching the informativeness of built-in property in 3.11+.

The factual claims check out: classproperty is applied to multiple properties on a single class (e.g. ByteConvertibleString in bittypes/string.py defines codepoint_changes, _reverse_codepoint_changes, _codepoint_change_regex, _reverse_codepoint_change_regex), so a bare "can't set attribute" would not disambiguate; and Python 3.11 did upgrade the built-in property to name the attribute, which this backport predates. So the finding is accurate, not a fabrication, and correctly scoped as low severity.

However, it leans nitpick and its practical impact is largely hypothetical, so I downgrade confidence: (1) These three strings are the verbatim pre-3.11 CPython property messages — a faithful, conventional backport idiom rather than author sloppiness. (2) classproperty is an internal utility used ONLY as a read-only getter throughout the codebase; no .setter/.deleter is ever applied, so the __set__/__delete__ branches (lines 45/51) and the fget-is-None getter branch (line 40) are effectively unreachable in current usage. The "developer hunting for which classproperty they touched" scenario therefore rarely, if ever, materializes. It is a legitimate, actionable low-severity polish suggestion (name the class/attribute to match 3.11+ property), but marginal in real-world value. Accept as real, keep severity low, lower confidence to reflect the mostly-unreachable error paths.
